A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ArTST study. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Arabic ASR experiments on pretraining, dialect-specific and joint fine-tuning, adaptation, and zero-shot transfer, with numerical results and appendix examples.

after.justification: v3 retains original dialectal experiments and adds multilingual/code-switching results and language-interference analyses, including Table 11, Figure 4, and appendix examples.

M1.justification: Both retain the SpeechT5/ArTST architecture, self-supervised pretraining, staged fine-tuning, and dialect-ID forcing/inference procedures. The new multilingual ArTST v3 variant is distinguished by its training data; no new architecture, loss, or decoding algorithm is documented.

E1.justification: v3 adds deliberate multilingual training using English, French, and Spanish CommonVoice data, and evaluates Egyptian-English ArzEn and Tunisian-French TunSwitch alongside the existing Emirati-English Mixat dataset. Tables 10 and 12 document substantially broader language and code-switching coverage.

E2.justification: v1 Table 6 reports Whisper and MMS comparisons on Mixat; that row disappears from v3 Table 5, while the new Mixat comparison in Table 11 contains ArTST variants. Comparator membership in the retained MGB benchmarks and other dialect comparisons is otherwise unchanged.

E3.justification: The new code-switching experiments compare direct target fine-tuning with initialization from different adapted checkpoints: MGB2 for ArTST v1, joint dialectal training for v2, and joint multilingual training for v3. v3 also adds multilingual-versus-dialectal evaluation on Arabic-only data. These are substantial additional experimental designs; the original splits, normalization, and basic evaluation metrics remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds explicit language-interference analysis on MSA and individual dialects, plus code-switching output comparisons across checkpoints and adaptation strategies. It removes v1 Figures 5–6, which illustrated zero-shot adaptation and held-out-dialect outputs. The original cross-dialect numerical analysis is retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or statistical significance tests. v3's use of 'significant' for performance differences does not introduce statistical testing.

E6.justification: New Table 11 reports adapted multilingual-model WERs of 27.43%, 36.66%, and 21.66% on ArzEn, TunSwitch, and Mixat. The retained adaptation table also changes values: MGB3 after MGB2 adaptation changes from 29.39 to 25.28, and Mixat after QASR adaptation from 27.73 to 35.21. Joint-dialect and cross-dialect matrices remain numerically unchanged. These are new results and reported revisions, without establishing same-setting rerun gains.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The dialect-prefixed decoding sequence and underlying conceptual framework are retained.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes dialectal pretraining, joint versus individual fine-tuning, and unseen-dialect generalization. v3 expands the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to claim multilingual code-switching capability, improved code-switching recognition, and a corresponding cost to monolingual performance. The contribution now explicitly includes dialectal and multilingual model releases.

C2.justification: v1 identifies limited code-switching recognition and unexplored multilingual/multidialectal training as limitations. v3 replaces that open question with an interpretation of measured tradeoffs: code-switching benefits, modest MSA degradation, and 4–16 percentage-point WER increases for some dialects, attributed to language interference. Existing limitations concerning coarse dialect labels and transcription variability remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies multilingual dataset inventories and quantities, estimates approximately 6,000 GPU-hours overall, and reports 14–21 days of pretraining per model instead of the earlier single 21-day description. It also expands the stated checkpoint and reproduction-script availability. Both versions already provide code links, optimizer settings, hardware, and normalization information.

R1.justification: Related work adds focused context on MSA-dominated research, distilled Arabic models, and code-switching, including Dhouib et al. (2022), Waheed et al. (2024), and Kadaoui et al. (2024), plus new dataset references. The central positioning around Arabic-specialized ArTST versus multilingual speech models remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of related work, methodology, and conclusions are rewritten around broader coverage. Methodology separates dialectal and multilingual fine-tuning, a code-switching section is introduced, and the cross-dialect discussion moves into a reorganized three-part appendix.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with axes, gridlines, and revised labeling. v3 adds multilingual data/results tables and an interference plot, replaces two earlier qualitative figures with code-switching examples, expands and relocates the pretraining table, and moves the cross-dialect matrix to Appendix C. These substantially revise the exhibit organization.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important gap explicitly acknowledged in v1: multilingual/code-switching training was unexplored. Section 8, Table 11, Figure 4, and appendix examples provide evidence across three code-switching datasets while exposing the cost to Arabic-only recognition, substantially improving the paper's account of coverage/performance tradeoffs. Reporting remains imperfect: a new sentence in Section 5.1 incorrectly says dialect forcing gives the lowest average WER, contradicting Table 7. The substantial empirical and interpretive gains outweigh this reporting regression.
